analysis.one_liner: Exempts tribal businesses on tribal land from federal labor law, removing workers' union rights there.
analysis.headline: The House committee approved it 22–16 and it sat on the House floor calendar for over a year, but it never received a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: Under federal labor law, most employers cannot punish workers for organizing and must bargain with a union their workers choose. This bill would carve tribal governments and any tribal business on tribal land — casinos, hotels, schools, hospitals — out of that law entirely. Supporters framed it as protecting tribal self-governance from a federal agency; it would also mean that workers at those enterprises, many of whom are not tribal members, lose their federal right to organize.
analysis.who_benefits: Tribal governments and the enterprises they own on tribal land would gain: they could no longer face unfair labor practice charges, union election petitions, or NLRB jurisdiction, giving them full control over workplace rules on their land [S2] [S4].

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds Indian tribes and tribal-owned enterprises on Indian lands to the National Labor Relations Act's definition of 'employer' — which means they would no longer be employers covered by the law's union and bargaining requirements [S2] [S4].

Supporters present this as a sovereignty matter: federally recognized tribes are governments, and the bill defines recognized tribes, tribal membership, and Indian lands — including former reservation boundaries in Oklahoma — to draw the exemption's lines [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Workers at tribal enterprises — casino and hotel staff, teachers, health workers, many of them non-Indian — would lose the federal protections against unfair labor practices and the right to form a union and bargain collectively [S2].

drawbacks.text: The bill removes, rather than adds, worker protections: employees at tribal businesses on tribal land would have no federal recourse if fired for organizing and no federal right to collective bargaining [S2].

Because the exemption covers enterprises owned by tribes on tribal land — including former Oklahoma reservations — businesses in labor-intensive industries like gaming and hospitality could operate without federal labor obligations, an uneven playing field against competing employers just off tribal land [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill advances a genuine constitutional principle — tribal self-governance — but its practical effect is to strip federal labor protections from the workforce of tribal enterprises, a workforce that includes large numbers of non-tribal members. Workers would have no federal backstop unless the tribe chose to provide one, and nothing in the bill requires tribes to replace those protections.

outcome.mechanism: The committee approved it on a 22–16 vote and put it on the House's floor calendar, but House leadership never brought it up for a vote, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce, which held a subcommittee hearing in March 2017 and marked it up in June 2017 [S6].
On June 29, 2017, the committee ordered the bill reported as amended on a 22–16 vote, and it was reported with amendments on September 25, 2017 [S6].
The same day it was reported, the bill was placed on the Union Calendar — the list of bills ready for floor action — but it never reached the House floor [S6].
The bill was never voted on by the House or Senate, and the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, killing it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employees at tribal enterprises kept their federal labor protections, and tribal employers remained subject to National Labor Relations Board jurisdiction, which a 2004 board decision had extended to tribal casinos and similar businesses. Unions and their members are better off than they would have been under the bill; tribal governments did not get the exemption they sought.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — 28 Republicans and 4 Democrats — but the committee vote that advanced it split 22–16 on party lines, and the bill never reached a floor vote where the full chamber would have weighed in.

industries.note: Casinos, hotels, and resorts owned by tribes on tribal land would be freed from NLRB jurisdiction, union election petitions, and unfair labor practice liability, giving them full control over workplace rules. The gain comes directly out of their employees' federal rights, so the industry's interest runs against the workers it employs.
Unions would lose the ability to organize workers at tribal enterprises on tribal land, one of the few sectors where non-union service jobs are concentrated on sovereign territory.

industries.industry: Other employers on tribal land (schools, hospitals, retail owned by tribes)
industries.note: Any tribal-owned institution on tribal land would be exempt, so tribal schools, clinics, and businesses would face no federal unfair-labor-practice liability. Their employees' federal protections would end with them.
